name: Fasting for face fat

card.summary: Intermittent fasting used to slim the face; trials show weight loss similar to ordinary calorie cutting, but nothing tests facial fat specifically.
card.note: No study has measured facial fat loss from fasting; fat loss sites are not chosen by the dieter, and health bodies advise against fasting for several groups.

quick.overview:
Fasting for face fat means using intermittent fasting (eating only in a window, alternate days, or occasional whole-day fasts) to lose body fat and, forum members hope, reveal a leaner face. It is discussed alongside cutting and 'leanmaxxing'.

Randomized trials and network meta-analyses show intermittent fasting can produce weight loss roughly comparable to continuous calorie restriction. No trial was found that measures facial fat, and forum members themselves disagree about hormonal downsides.
quick.mechanism: Fasting regimens reduce calorie intake and prolong overnight fasting intervals; reviews propose effects via circadian biology, gut microbiome and sleep. How fat is lost from different body regions varies by person and genetics, and forum posters report people with low body fat but fuller faces.
quick.risks: Short-term hunger, irritability, dizziness and headache are reported; fasting is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children, underweight people or those prone to eating disorders. Forum members worry about effects on testosterone, thyroid and muscle, while a 2025 Cell study reported that intermittent fasting suppressed hair follicle regeneration.

lead: Fasting for face fat is the use of intermittent fasting patterns, such as daily time-restricted eating, alternate-day fasting or 5:2 schedules, with the aim of lowering body fat and thereby slimming the face.[1][2] It sits within looksmaxxing discussions of cutting, 'leanmaxxing' and hollow-cheek aesthetics.[3]

A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 99 randomized trials in 6,582 adults compared intermittent fasting with continuous energy restriction and unrestricted eating for body weight and cardiometabolic outcomes.[4] Reviews generally describe weight loss similar to ordinary calorie restriction, and the American Heart Association and National Institute on Aging have described evidence for broader benefits as limited.[1][5] No study has measured facial fat after fasting.
infobox: About 2.5% to 9.9% of body weight (per Wikipedia)

paras: Intermittent fasting covers time-restricted eating (a daily window of often 8 to 12 hours), alternate-day fasting, the 5:2 diet of two low-calorie days a week, and periodic water-only fasts beyond 24 hours.[1] Therapeutic fasting for obesity was studied as early as 1915 and attracted renewed medical interest in the 1960s.[1]
In looksmaxxing communities the interest is usually in reaching low body fat to define the jaw and cheeks, sometimes combined with exercise.[3][6]

Proponents describe fasting as an easy way to cut calories and lose body fat, and some cite research on autophagy and hair growth, noting that exercise and fasting may promote autophagy in follicles.[7] Forum members debating benefits and harms point to possible declines in IGF-1, testosterone and thyroid hormones and to hunger-related stress hormones as downsides.[8]

The 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis found intermittent fasting strategies to be a viable weight-loss approach, with results generally comparable to continuous energy restriction.[4] Reviews describe improvements in some cardiometabolic markers and hypothesize roles for circadian biology, the gut microbiome and sleep.[9][10]

An early time-restricted feeding trial in men with prediabetes reported better insulin sensitivity, blood pressure and oxidative stress even without weight loss.[11] A trial in resistance-trained men tested 16/8 time-restricted feeding on body composition and strength.[12]

Wikipedia reports that the US National Institute on Aging calls the research limited and inconclusive and does not recommend intermittent fasting for the general public, that fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance, and that reported short-term side effects include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea and headaches.[1]
A 2025 Cell paper reported that intermittent fasting suppressed hair follicle regeneration through inter-organ signaling, a finding relevant to forum concerns about hair.[13]

No published study was found that measures facial fat change from fasting. Forum threads describe people with low body fat who retain a fuller face and ask whether genetics explains it, while others report that continued leaning improved their face.[14][15]

No studies found of fasting for facial fat specifically. Human trials of intermittent fasting examine body weight, glucose control, blood pressure and lipids, including a 2025 network meta-analysis of 99 randomized trials and trials in people with type 2 diabetes.[4][16][17]

timeline.event: Therapeutic fasting for obesity studied (per Wikipedia).[1]
Controlled trial of early time-restricted feeding in men with prediabetes.[11]
NEJM review of intermittent fasting, health, aging and disease.[18]
BMJ network meta-analysis of intermittent fasting trials; Cell paper on fasting and hair follicle regeneration.[4][13]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, intermittent fasting is discussed as a weight-loss tool, a possible hair-health aid via autophagy, and a possible hormonal risk.[7][8]

claims.claim: Fasting slims the face by cutting body fat
claims.believers: Posters report losing body fat with fasting and expect a leaner face.[6]
claims.experts: Trials show weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction, but no study measures facial fat.[4]

claims.claim: Fasting and exercise promote autophagy that prevents balding
claims.believers: A thread summarizing a video argues autophagy is needed for hair growth and recommends fasting, exercise and metformin.[7]
claims.experts: Laboratory papers link autophagy to hair follicles, while a 2025 Cell study reported fasting suppressed hair follicle regeneration; no trial shows fasting prevents balding.[13]

claims.claim: Fasting lowers testosterone, thyroid and hair health
claims.believers: Posters say fasting reduces IGF-1, testosterone and thyroid hormones and raises cortisol.[8]
claims.experts: Reviews describe mostly metabolic effects and call longer-term outcomes under-studied; short-term side effects are hunger and irritability.[1][9]

claims.believers: A forum thread asks whether intermittent fasting will lose muscle.[19]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes weight lost on fasting is mostly fat but includes some lean mass; a trial of 16/8 feeding in resistance-trained men studied strength and body composition.[1][12]
